chapter_title: Construction and Design Verification for Unbound Pavement Materials

sections.title: Construction Specifications (Method, Result, Performance) and Corrective Action
sections.summary: Specifications tie the design intent to the finished product and are generally categorized as method (prescribes equipment and procedure - e.g. 4 passes of a 35-ton sheepsfoot roller per 8-in. lift), result (prescribes a property to achieve - e.g. 95% of maximum dry density by AASHTO T99, giving the contractor latitude in process), or performance (defines materials/quality characteristics that correlate with long-term performance). The result specification is the most common; the method specification is used where the result is probable from local experience or hard to measure (e.g. coarse rock fill). With respect to geotechnical factors, every specification aims to confirm or improve soil/aggregate behavior by adjusting moisture content and densifying (compacting), and emphasizes raw-material properties (classification, max particle size, gradation, Atterberg limits, toughness, soundness). Each specification should include corrective-action provisions for unsuitable (weak, soft, wet, yielding) conditions: detection method, treatment depth, treatment type (drainage, undercut-and-replace, geosynthetics, chemical modification/stabilization), and pay responsibility.
sections.body: Specifications dictate the quality of the constructed pavement section, tying design intent to performance; there is no good practice other than what is specified in the contract. Most agencies adopt guideline specifications (e.g. AASHTO Standard Specifications for Transportation Materials) modified for local conditions, materials, techniques, and experience. Specifications are categorized as METHOD (describes in detail the equipment and procedures to achieve a result - e.g. 4 passes of a 35-ton sheepsfoot roller, Caterpillar C825 or equivalent, on each 8-in. loose lift), RESULT (states the property to be achieved, allowing the contractor to innovate the process - e.g. 95% of maximum dry density by AASHTO T99 standard Proctor on each lift), or PERFORMANCE (key materials and construction-quality characteristics demonstrated to correlate with long-term performance - e.g. support 1 million ESALs without fatigue cracks or rut depths exceeding 6 mm (0.25 in.)). Performance specifications take three forms (Chamberlin, 1995): performance specifications (directly define road condition/response/material condition at a given time), performance-based specifications (desired levels of fundamental engineering properties that predict performance), and performance-related specifications (key materials/construction characteristics correlated with long-term performance). With respect to geotechnical factors, each specification type aims to confirm the adequacy of, or improve, the soil/aggregate engineering behavior by modifying moisture content and densifying (compacting) the material. The result specification is more common and encourages the most efficient/economical means; the method specification is used where the result is probable from local experience or hard to measure (e.g. density of coarse rock fill), but it shifts responsibility from the contractor to the owner/engineer. Performance specifications suit design/build and warranty contracts but cannot directly control aggregate or subgrade material quality, since the pavement is an interdependent layered system whose properties change over service life and whose performance also depends on layer thickness (a design element). Regardless of type, a specification should emphasize raw-material properties (soil classification, maximum particle size, gradation, Atterberg limits, toughness/durability, soundness) and should contain corrective-action provisions for unsuitable (weak, soft, wet, yielding) conditions, specifying the method of detection (proofroll, QC/QA test), depth of anticipated treatment, type of treatment (drainage, undercut-and-replace, geosynthetics, chemical modification/stabilization), and a quick resolution of pay responsibility (owner vs. contractor).
key_points: Specification ties design intent to finished product; three types: method, result, performance
Method: prescribes equipment + procedure; Result: prescribes a property (e.g. 95% of max dry density, AASHTO T99); Performance: ties to long-term field performance
Result spec is most common; method spec used where result is probable locally or hard to measure (coarse rock fill)
Geotechnical intent of every spec: confirm/improve soil-aggregate behavior via moisture adjustment + densification
Emphasize raw-material properties: classification, max particle size, gradation, Atterberg limits, toughness, soundness
Include corrective-action provisions: detection method, treatment depth, treatment type (drainage / undercut-replace / geosynthetics / chemical stabilization), pay responsibility

sections.title: QC/QA Traditional Methods - Proof Rolling and Field Density/Moisture Testing
sections.summary: Good quality control/quality assurance (QC/QA) is essential. QC is the contractor's (or third-party) field testing/observation per a QC Plan; QA is the owner's verification that the plan is followed. Material-source tests (classification, Atterberg limits, gradation, moisture-density/Proctor, abrasion, soundness) are run per material type, and field installation tests (moisture content, density, stiffness/proof rolling) per the QC Plan (Table 8-1). Proof rolling points out soft or yielding material by driving a heavy specified vehicle over the embankment, prepared subgrade (top 300 mm/12 in.), or completed base/subbase and watching for excessive deflection; agencies set weight, tire pressure, and deflection-threshold criteria. Detected soft zones (which can pass density but fail on moisture) are delineated (penetration rods, hand augers) and remediated by undercut/replace, underdrains, geosynthetics, or chemical stabilization. Traditional in-place tests are nuclear density (Figure 8-1), sand cone, balloon, and drive tube, with moisture by nuclear gauge, speedy moisture, or oven drying. Process control of density/moisture trends along the alignment (Figure 8-2) can reveal that out-of-tolerance density is actually driven by out-of-control moisture.
sections.body: Good QC/QA practices are essential for satisfactory results. Quality control (QC) is field observation/testing performed by a third party, the agency, or - per a written QC Plan submitted by the contractor and approved by the owner/engineer - by the contractor, covering material production/purchase and proper installation. The QC Plan includes tests on materials at a prescribed frequency (Table 8-1) plus field compaction monitoring/control. Quality assurance (QA) documents that the contractor is following the QC Plan, typically via random inspection and verification testing. Table 8-1 lists material-source tests run once per material type (classification, Atterberg limits, grain size, moisture-density/Proctor, abrasion, soundness) and field-installation tests run per the QC Plan (moisture content, density, stiffness assessment such as proof rolling). PROOF ROLLING: the objective is to point out soft or yielding material; it can be applied during embankment construction, subgrade preparation (top 300 mm (12 in.)), and completion of base/subbase, and observations can be made with the excavation, hauling, placing, and compaction equipment in use. Many agencies specify vehicle weight and tire pressure and set deflection thresholds for acceptable vs. remediation-requiring zones (e.g. Ohio uses proof rolling for new, rehabilitation, and reconstruction projects). Proof rolling detects soft zones that may have passed density but not moisture-content requirements, and can reveal problems extending many feet below the surface; once detected, the depth is estimated (experience, penetration rods, hand augers), delineated in aerial extent and depth, and remediated (remove/undercut and replace, underdrains, geosynthetics, chemical stabilization) per cost/schedule constraints. A field-monitoring checklist (Table 8-2) covers reading specifications, reviewing plans (lines, grades, layer thickness, drainage, corrective-action requirements), checking site conditions (clearing/grubbing, deflection under load, proof rolling/DCP foundation acceptance), and on-site monitoring/testing (hauling/placement/spreading adequacy, moisture reasonableness, compaction effort and testing, stabilizing-agent rate and mixing). TESTS: in-place QC/acceptance traditionally relies on nuclear density measurement (Figure 8-1), sand cone, balloon, or drive-tube methods, with moisture by nuclear gauge, speedy moisture, or hot-plate/oven drying, performed on embankment fill, finished subgrade, and unbound base (and some chemically stabilized materials). Practice has shifted from method-calibration plus observation toward statistical characterization with random sampling and pay factors. PROCESS CONTROL: tracking a measured value (or its trend) over time can explain why another process is out of compliance. In the Figure 8-2 example, density is adequate over the first 120 m (400 ft) then trends out of control; the moisture data reveal that moisture (not compactive effort) is the out-of-control parameter, and spreading thinner lifts to allow drying returns the work to satisfactory by the 250 m (820 ft) mark. This density/moisture process control applies to embankment, subgrade, and unbound aggregate base; gradation of aggregate base is also an important process-control measure (detecting segregation/contamination and confirming quarry control).
key_points: QC = contractor/third-party field testing per QC Plan; QA = owner verification that the plan is followed
Material-source tests per material type; field tests (moisture, density, proof rolling) per QC Plan (Table 8-1)
Proof rolling points out soft/yielding material on embankment, subgrade (top 300 mm/12 in.), and base/subbase
Soft zones can pass density but fail moisture; delineate (rods/augers) then undercut-replace, underdrain, geosynthetics, or stabilize
Traditional in-place tests: nuclear density (Figure 8-1), sand cone, balloon, drive tube; moisture by nuclear/speedy/oven
Process control of density and moisture trends along alignment (Figure 8-2) shows moisture often drives out-of-control density
Field-monitoring checklist (Table 8-2) guides inspection of site prep, materials, compaction, and stabilization

sections.title: QC/QA Emerging Technologies - Verifying Stiffness Design Intent
sections.summary: Traditional acceptance measures density, but the design intent for subgrade and unbound layers is stiffness/strength (resilient modulus, CBR, k-value) - and density does not necessarily confirm stiffness, since a soil can meet the compaction specification on the wet side of optimum yet be too soft. Several measures verify the stiffness design intent directly: field CBR (for flexible, in-situ CBR) and plate load (for rigid, modulus of subgrade reaction k - the European standard), Dynamic Cone Penetration (DCP, with CBR < 6 expected to rut under construction and 6-8 marginally suitable), resilient-modulus testing on Shelby-tube samples of finished subgrade, and nondestructive testing (FWD, portable lightweight deflectometer LWD - Figure 8-3, GeoGauge for direct stiffness, and seismic PSPA/DSPA). Real-time automatic controlled variable roller compaction (intelligent compaction) uses drum accelerometers to measure soil dynamic stiffness during compaction, automatically adjusting energy and providing 100% coverage that enables performance-based specifications and warranties.
sections.body: Most projects accept the contractor's earthwork on a result specification of density, but the design intent for the subgrade and unbound layers is stiffness/strength (resilient modulus near final grade; shear strength and consolidation for the embankment fill below). Density does not verify that design intent: a contractor can meet the compaction specification on the wet side of optimum and still fall short of the required stiffness. In the chapter's hypothetical (Boudreau, 2003), a roadbed design-intent stiffness of about 50 MPa (about 7200 psi) is set for five soils (Table 8-3, ranging from sandy SC/A-4 to highly plastic CH/A-7-6), each compacted to 95% of maximum dry density at optimum moisture (AASHTO T99); the question is whether meeting that density actually delivers the design stiffness. Several measures verify design intent directly: FIELD CBR and PLATE LOAD TESTS (field CBR gives in-situ CBR of finished subgrade for flexible pavements; the plate load test directly measures the modulus of subgrade reaction k for rigid pavements and is the European standard, but both are time-consuming and little used in the U.S.); DYNAMIC CONE PENETRATION (DCP - a steel shaft with an instrumented penetration head per Table 4-9, measuring resistance per increment and correlated to stiffness/strength; quickly mobilized and able to profile below the surface, but giving discrete points and correlation-dependent values; an estimated in-situ CBR <= 6 is expected to rut/deflect under construction, and 6-8 is marginally suitable for construction support); RESILIENT MODULUS TESTING on short Shelby-tube samples extracted from the compacted finished subgrade; and NONDESTRUCTIVE TESTING (NDT) including lasers, ground-penetrating radar, falling weight deflectometer (FWD), portable/lightweight deflectometer (LWD, Figure 8-3, less than 4 minutes per location), GeoGauge (direct composite-soil stiffness at discrete points), and seismic methods (the Portable Seismic Pavement Analyzer PSPA and its base/subgrade derivative DSPA, akin to SASW). PROOF ROLLING remains a practical, observer-dependent screen for gross deficiencies (soft, yielding, pumping subgrade), with newer laser/digital-video systems enabling near-direct deflection measurement (e.g. Wisconsin DOT used a 38 mm (1.5 in.) deflection threshold for failed areas). INTELLIGENT COMPACTION: the real-time automatic controlled variable roller compaction and documentation system uses drum accelerometers to monitor the dynamic-wave speed and measure soil dynamic stiffness (which rises with compaction), automatically adjusting compaction energy via two counter-rotating drum weights and providing measurement/documentation feedback. Its key value is continuous 100% quality-control coverage of the entire project, which enables performance-based specifications and the effective implementation of earthwork and pavement warranties. RISK ACCEPTANCE: extending warranties from the standard 1 year to 2-5 years shifts performance risk from owner to contractor, motivating contractor involvement in design and more sophisticated life-cycle monitoring.
key_points: Design intent for subgrade/unbound layers is stiffness/strength (Mr, CBR, k), but acceptance traditionally measures density
Density does not confirm stiffness - compaction can be met wet of optimum yet be too soft
Field CBR (flexible) and plate load test for k (rigid, European standard) verify design intent directly
DCP correlates to CBR/stiffness; CBR <= 6 expected to rut under construction, 6-8 marginally suitable (Table 4-9)
Resilient-modulus testing on Shelby-tube samples of finished subgrade verifies the design value
NDT: FWD, lightweight deflectometer LWD (Figure 8-3), GeoGauge (direct stiffness), seismic PSPA/DSPA
Intelligent compaction: drum accelerometers measure dynamic stiffness, give 100% coverage, enable performance specs and warranties
Longer (2-5 yr) warranties shift performance risk toward the contractor

sections.title: Subgrade Preparation, Drainage, Excavation, and Hauling/Placement
sections.summary: Pavement construction grades the support layers to design elevation, ideally balancing cut and fill. For new construction, subgrade prep needs clearing and grubbing to remove vegetation, debris, and organic/soft/unsuitable material before grading or placing fill; for reconstruction the old surface (and unsuitable base/subbase) is removed. Rutting/deflection under heavy equipment is the first sign of weak soil; if unanticipated soft material is found, conditions must be improved by (1) remove and replace with select material, (2) stabilize in place (Chapter 7 techniques), or (3) improve drainage. Excess water is the principal cause of instability, so dewatering or stabilization is often better than undercutting large areas. Construction underdrains can be installed promptly to gain significant subgrade stability; soils saturated above 80-90% within ~1 m (2-4 ft), or saturated soils with more than 10% fines, will not support construction traffic by drainage alone and may need evaporation/aeration. Excavation uses scrapers and track-mounted excavators; hauled fill (including off-site borrow) is sampled and Proctor-tested, and observed for soft areas.
sections.body: Construction of the pavement involves grading to provide uniform support at the design elevation, using equipment to excavate, haul, add or remove water, spread, and compact, ideally with a balance of site materials (cut deficits require off-site borrow; cut surpluses are wasted). For NEW CONSTRUCTION, subgrade preparation typically requires grubbing and grading (cut or fill); clearing and grubbing to remove vegetation, debris, and organic/soft/unsuitable material from the surface (at subgrade level or before placing fill) is very important, since long-term performance problems are often traced to inadequate removal of unsuitable materials (organic surface soils are moisture-sensitive, lose strength when wet, and disturb easily). For RECONSTRUCTION, the old roadway surface is removed (possibly recycled) along with base/subbase if unsuitable (e.g. intermixed with fines). Observation of heavy-equipment operation gives the first indication of subgrade adequacy: rutting and deflection during initial earthwork signal an immediate problem (acceptable only if undercut or stabilization was anticipated). To improve unsuitable soil conditions, three options are common: (1) remove marginal soils and replace with select higher-quality material; (2) stabilize in-place soil (Chapter 7 techniques); or (3) improve site drainage. Removal-and-replacement seems easiest and works for small/spot areas, but undercutting large areas may be undesirable; since excess water is the principal cause of unstable conditions, dewatering or stabilization may better expedite construction (hauling/loading on a wet subgrade continually disturbs it, and wet-condition excavation begets more excavation). Other earthwork concerns include settlement of natural soils under large embankments (analyze settlement potential; mitigate by remove-and-replace or surcharge), and rare construction over voids/weak zones (caves, faults, abandoned mines, sinkholes) detected by GPR or SASW (Chapter 4) and mitigated by excavation/backfill, injection grouting, grout columns, or bridging with reinforced slabs/geogrid-reinforced base. DRAINAGE (8.4.1): if wet/saturated conditions or clogged existing underdrains are found, drainage work should start as soon as possible. Cleaning existing underdrain outlets (rehabilitation) and adding construction underdrains (new construction) significantly improves subgrade stability, often reducing pumping within a few days. Soils that densify and are not free-draining (saturation exceeding 80-90%) within about 1 m (2-4 ft) of the surface are not expected to support construction traffic, and saturated soils with more than 10% fines (minus No. 200) are not drainable enough to support construction traffic - moisture reduction by evaporation (disking, aeration) may then be more feasible than gravity drainage. Construction underdrains are usually placed at the roadway centerline (or in the ditch line for cut-section inflow), are sacrificial (continue working even after the upper backfill is contaminated), and in rock/shale cuts the design underdrains should extend at least 150 mm (6 in.) into the rock to prevent water accumulating at the rock-soil interface. EXCAVATION (8.4.2): removal of in-situ soil to grade, typically with scrapers (pans) or track-mounted excavators (shovels); vertical movement below the equipment is the first QC sign of weak soils, and wet/saturated conditions may require shovels (less disturbance) over scrapers. HAULING AND PLACEMENT (8.4.3): scrapers move their own payload while shovels need haul trucks (end/side/bottom/articulated dump); off-site borrow is dumped near its final location and spread by dozer or motor grader. Excessive rutting calls for changed haul routes and an assessment of underdrain need - well-timed construction underdrains can mitigate, and hauling over a previously unstable, now-draining area can add compaction. Fill material is sampled and tested for compliance during hauling, and laboratory moisture-density (Proctor) tests are run for correlation with field density testing.
key_points: Grade to design elevation with a balance of cut and fill; clearing/grubbing removes organic/soft/unsuitable material
Rutting/deflection under heavy equipment is the first indication of weak subgrade
Improve unsuitable soil by (1) remove-and-replace, (2) in-place stabilization (Chapter 7), or (3) drainage
Excess water is the principal cause of instability - dewatering/stabilization often beats undercutting large areas
Construction underdrains (centerline; sacrificial) markedly improve subgrade stability, often within days
Saturation > 80-90% within ~1 m (2-4 ft), or saturated soil with > 10% fines, will not support construction traffic by drainage alone
Rock/shale cuts: underdrains extend >= 150 mm (6 in.) into rock to avoid water at the rock-soil interface
Excavation by scrapers/excavators; haul-fill is Proctor-tested and observed for soft areas
Large embankments need settlement analysis (mitigate by remove-replace or surcharge); voids/sinkholes detected by GPR/SASW

sections.title: Field Compaction - Equipment, Lift Thickness, and Moisture Control
sections.summary: Compaction is densification by mechanical energy, usually with moisture adjustment, to maximize strength and minimize settlement and volume change. Optimal engineering properties occur near the laboratory optimum moisture content (OMC), where void ratio and shrink/swell potential are minimized; field density is controlled against the matching laboratory moisture-density standard (AASHTO T99 standard or T180 modified Proctor), with high-energy equipment controlled by the modified Proctor. Equipment is matched to soil type (Table 8-4): smooth/vibratory drum rollers for granular cohesionless soils, sheepsfoot/padfoot (kneading) rollers for plastic cohesive soils, pneumatic rubber-tired for both (especially silty), and high-energy impact rollers for greater depth (Figure 8-15). Compaction is done in lifts of 150-300 mm (6-12 in.), up to ~0.7 m (2 ft) with high-energy equipment and free-draining soils. A firm foundation is essential - a thin lift over a weak subgrade gets low roller stress and poor compaction, and high stresses in the soft soil can cause shear failure (Figure 8-11). Compact at OMC; if deviating, err to the wet side.
sections.body: Compaction is the densification of soils by mechanical energy, often requiring modification of water content, to enhance strength/load capacity while minimizing long-term settlement; adjusting moisture to near optimum reduces volume change and increases strength. Optimal engineering properties for a soil occur near its laboratory optimum moisture content (OMC or wopt), where void ratio and shrink (if dried)/swell (if inundated) potential are minimized. Field moisture and density are measured by standard methods and correlated to the laboratory moisture-density relationship (AASHTO T99 standard Proctor, T180 modified Proctor; moisture-density behavior is discussed in Chapter 7 and the lab tests in Chapter 5). The appropriate laboratory method must be matched to the local equipment energy - higher-energy field equipment should be controlled by the modified (not standard) Proctor. There is a trend toward lower moisture tolerances to suit higher-energy equipment, but compacting above optimum with high-energy equipment causes apparent pumping, and over-aggressive moisture limits can yield lower compactive effort and premature failure as the subgrade later saturates (loss of stiffness/strength, volume change). It is good practice to compact at the OMC; if some deviation occurs it is better to be on the wet side than the dry. Compaction (mechanical stabilization) is the most common and least expensive soil-improvement technique, and the most common construction problem; deficient compaction (e.g. in utility trenches and bridge abutments where vertical constraints hinder compaction) causes localized settlement and surface cracking, avoidable with attention to moisture content, lift thickness, and equipment configuration (weight and width are most critical). EQUIPMENT (Table 8-4): compaction is by pressure, vibration, and/or kneading. Smooth drum rollers (often with oscillatory vibrators; Figure 8-12) suit granular, relatively non-cohesive soils; sheepsfoot/studded (padfoot) rollers (Figure 8-13) impart high contact pressure and a kneading/shearing action that compacts cohesive soils from the bottom up and maximizes their strength; pneumatic rubber-tired rollers suit a variety of soils and are particularly effective for non-cohesive silty soils; and high-energy impact rollers with shaped (triangular/hexagonal) drums (Figure 8-14) compact faster and to greater depth (Figure 8-15). Low-ground-pressure equipment (bulldozers, loaders, graders) is ineffective for compaction, though tracked vehicles give limited vibratory compaction of granular soils. Recommended first/second choices by soil type (Table 8-4): vibratory for rock fill and clean sands/gravels (A-1); sheepsfoot/padfoot for plastic (CH/MH, A-7/A-5, thin lifts) and low-plasticity (CL/ML, A-6/A-4, moisture control critical for silts) soils; vibratory/pneumatic for plastic sands and gravels (GC/SC) and silty sands/gravels (SM/GM). LIFT THICKNESS: the effective compaction depth is limited, so thick fills are built in lifts of 150-300 mm (6-12 in.), up to about 0.7 m (2 ft) with specialized high-energy equipment and free-draining granular soils; soil type, required degree of compaction, field energy (equipment and number of passes), and operator skill set the maximum effective lift, and water content of each lift may need drying or wetting plus mixing. FOUNDATION SUPPORT: satisfactory compaction is difficult if the lift is not on a firm foundation - Figure 8-11 shows that the roller-induced stresses in a 150 mm (6 in.) lift of 170 MPa (25,000 psi) granular material over a soft 35 MPa (5,000 psi) subgrade (CBR ~3-4) are much lower than over a uniform stiff deposit, so high compaction is hard to achieve and high stresses in the soft soil can cause shear failure and excessive rutting (especially under proof rolling). Proof rolling with heavy rubber-tired rollers gives additional compaction and identifies soft areas, but the proof roller must be sized to avoid bearing-capacity failures and is not a substitute for good compaction and inspection. The final phase of subgrade construction is confirming surficial support before placing base/subbase, using proof rolling, DCP, or FWD (Section 8.3). Deep densification (dynamic compaction, vibroflotation; FHWA NHI-04-001) can densify loose non-cohesive soils (sands/gravels) below ~9 m (30 ft).
key_points: Compaction = densification by mechanical energy + moisture control; best properties near laboratory OMC
Control field density vs. matched lab standard: AASHTO T99 (standard) or T180 (modified) Proctor; modified for high-energy equipment
Compact at OMC; if deviating, err wet rather than dry
Equipment by soil (Table 8-4): smooth/vibratory drum for granular, sheepsfoot/padfoot (kneading) for plastic cohesive, pneumatic for both/silty, impact for depth
Lifts of 150-300 mm (6-12 in.), up to ~0.7 m (2 ft) with high-energy equipment on free-draining soils
A firm foundation is essential - thin lift over soft subgrade gets low roller stress and risks shear failure (Figure 8-11)
Proof roller must be sized to avoid bearing-capacity failure; confirm subgrade by proof roll/DCP/FWD before base placement
Deep densification (dynamic compaction, vibroflotation) for loose non-cohesive soils (FHWA NHI-04-001)

sections.title: Chemical Stabilization and Base/Subbase Construction
sections.summary: When stabilization is economical, chemical admixtures (lime, flyash, cement) are used; the mixture (admixture content, max density, OMC, strength) is designed in the laboratory (Chapter 7). The four basic construction steps are (1) pozzolan delivery/distribution, (2) mixing, (3) compacting, and (4) curing. Lime is applied dry (hydrated lime - fine, dusty; or quicklime - granular, less dusty) or as a slurry. Adequate mixing (disking, blading, rotary or pug-mill mixers) is critical - poor mixing is the leading cause of unsatisfactory results - and a two-stage mix is used for highly plastic soils. Lime addition lowers maximum density and raises optimum water content, so in-situ lime-soil compaction curves may be needed for density control. Curing above 4.4 C (40 F) with adequate moisture for 3-7 days (moist or asphalt-seal curing) is essential for the pozzolanic strength gain. For aggregate base/subbase, material is placed on grade, spread to uniform thickness, and compacted while minimizing segregation and contamination from site soil.
sections.body: CHEMICAL STABILIZATION (8.4.5): where stabilization is a more economical way to achieve the desired support, chemical admixtures such as lime, flyash, or cement are used; the mixture is designed in a controlled laboratory environment to establish volumetric properties - admixture design content, maximum density, moisture content, and strength (Chapter 7). The basic construction steps for chemical stabilization of subgrade soils are (1) pozzolan delivery and distribution, (2) mixing, (3) compacting, and (4) curing. Pozzolans are applied dry or as a slurry: dry lime is either fine-grained hydrated lime (dust-control problems) or granular dry quicklime (much less dusty), distributed by manually spread bags, pneumatic trucks with spreader bars, or dump trucks with controlled tailgate openings; lime slurry is batched centrally or in portable systems (a typical mix is 0.9 tonne (1 ton) of lime in 1900 liters (500 gal) of water). Adequate mixing of the pozzolan with the soil is critical - poor mixing is the leading cause of unsatisfactory stabilization - and is done by disking, repeated blading, or traveling rotary/pug-mill mixers (Figure 8-16), usually in thin lifts with multiple passes; a two-stage mixing process is sometimes used for highly plastic materials, since the reduced plasticity and coarser texture developing during several days of curing after the initial mix improves workability for final mixing and compaction. Compaction of stabilized mixtures follows standard procedures, but adding lime generally decreases the maximum density and increases the optimum water content, so compaction curves of the in-situ lime-soil mixture at the time of compaction may be needed to set the field density-control target. Curing at temperatures above 4.4 C (40 F) with adequate moisture is essential for the pozzolanic reactions behind long-term strength gain; a 3-7 day cure period is typical, with moisture maintained by moist curing (truck sprinklers) or an asphalt seal. Modified soil (lime, cement, and/or flyash) requires special QC/QA (Section 8.3), and the stabilized subgrade surface should be evaluated by proof rolling, DCP, or FWD. Additional stabilization QC controls (Section 8.3.1) include pulverization/scarification (field-sieve sampling at 25 mm (1 in.) and 4.75 mm (No. 4)), stabilizing-agent content (canvas-area sampling, or pH for lime dosage per Appendix E), uniformity of mixing (visual, with phenolphthalein indicator turning lime-treated soil pink to show treatment depth), compaction/moisture control, and curing (moist or membrane/bituminous, fully sealed). BASE AND SUBBASE CONSTRUCTION (8.4.6): aggregate base is hauled to the site, placed directly on grade, spread to a uniform specified thickness, and compacted, with care to minimize segregation (reduce transfer points and intermediate stockpiling; minimize on-grade spreading/movement; asphalt spreaders give good thickness control and reduce segregation). Care is also needed to avoid contaminating the aggregate with site soil, which typically occurs when wet soils adhere to construction-traffic tires/tracks and are deposited on newly placed aggregate; QC/QA personnel document conformance/non-conformance.
key_points: Chemical admixtures (lime, flyash, cement) designed in the lab for content, max density, OMC, strength (Chapter 7)
Four construction steps: (1) pozzolan delivery/distribution, (2) mixing, (3) compacting, (4) curing
Lime applied dry (hydrated - dusty; quicklime - granular) or as slurry; adequate mixing is critical (poor mixing is leading failure cause)
Two-stage mixing for highly plastic soils; phenolphthalein indicates lime treatment depth
Lime lowers max density and raises optimum water content - use in-situ lime-soil compaction curves for control
Cure above 4.4 C (40 F) with moisture for 3-7 days (moist or asphalt-seal curing) for pozzolanic strength gain
Confirm stabilized surface by proof roll / DCP / FWD
Aggregate base/subbase: place on grade, spread to uniform thickness, compact; minimize segregation and contamination from site soil
